## What is a quality management system in a contact center?


A quality management system is a structured framework of processes, tools, and standards that organizations use to monitor, evaluate, and improve the quality of service delivery. In a contact center, a QMS provides the operational structure for recording customer interactions, scoring agent performance against defined criteria, and connecting evaluation results to coaching and improvement programs.


In a contact center context, a QMS is the operational backbone of service quality. It defines what "good" looks like through scorecards and evaluation criteria, and gives supervisors the mechanism to measure agent interactions against those standards. A well-designed quality management system for customer service teams connects evaluation data directly to coaching outcomes, so performance improvement becomes systematic rather than ad hoc.


Historically, quality management relied on supervisors manually reviewing a small sample of recorded calls. Modern QMS platforms use AI to analyze a much larger share of interactions across voice and digital channels, surfacing insights that manual review alone may miss at scale. That shift from sample-based to more comprehensive interaction coverage is one of the defining changes in how contact centers manage service quality today.


## What are the key QMS features?


The strongest quality management systems do more than score calls — they connect evaluation data to coaching, compliance, and improvement workflows. Here are the core capabilities to assess when evaluating QMS software:


- **Interaction recording and transcription.** Captures voice and digital conversations across your supported channels (voice, chat, email, and messaging) and converts them into searchable, reviewable records.
- **Customizable Evaluation Forms.** Defines the evaluation criteria that matter to your operation, from compliance adherence to communication skills and issue resolution.
- **AI-powered evaluation.** Automatically scores interactions against your scorecard criteria, giving supervisors visibility across a far greater volume of conversations than manual methods allow.
- **Sentiment analysis.** Analyzes sentiment indicators within conversations to help supervisors prioritize interactions that may need immediate attention.
- **Coaching and feedback workflows.** Routes evaluation results to targeted[coaching workflows](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/skip-manual-workforce-management-and-coaching/) , so performance feedback reaches the right agent at the right time.
- **Performance dashboards and analytics.** Aggregates evaluation data into team- and individual-level trend reports, giving managers a clear view of how to improve agent performance with quality management over time.
- **Compliance monitoring.** Flags interactions that may contain compliance risks — such as missed disclosures or policy deviations — for supervisor review.


A modern QMS works best when it integrates natively with your contact center platform rather than operating as a separate system, so evaluation data and interaction records stay connected without manual effort.[Zoom Quality Management](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/quality-management/) is built as a native add-on to Zoom Contact Center, keeping all quality management workflows on the same platform where customer interactions happen.

## How do you choose QMS software?


Selecting QMS software involves more than comparing feature lists. Contact center managers need a system that fits their team's workflows, scales with their interaction volume, and integrates with their existing technology stack. Use these criteria to guide your evaluation:


1. **Assess interaction coverage.** Determine what percentage of your interactions the QMS can evaluate and at what cost. A system that evaluates only a small sample leaves significant performance data invisible.
2. **Evaluate omnichannel support.** Your customers interact across voice, chat, email, and messaging. Your QMS should capture and evaluate all those channels consistently, not just phone calls.
3. **Review scorecard flexibility.** Look for a system that lets you build and adjust evaluation criteria to match your specific compliance requirements, service standards, and performance goals.
4. **Assess platform integration.** A QMS that requires manual data exports or separate logins creates friction for supervisors. This is a common limitation of legacy, bolt-on quality management tools that were never built to leverage the value of AI or provide real-time insight across channels. Look for a solution built into, or deeply integrated with, your core contact center platform.
5. **Evaluate AI capabilities and governance.** AI-powered scoring accelerates evaluation at scale — but for HR, compliance, and workforce teams, the question isn't just what AI can score. It's who owns the result. Confirm that supervisors can review, calibrate, and override AI-generated scores, and that the vendor can show you how disputes or miscalibrations are handled. In regulated environments or unionized workforces, this isn't a nice-to-have. It's a prerequisite.
6. **Consider coaching workflow support.** Evaluation data is only useful if it reaches agents in a timely, actionable way. Assess how the QMS connects evaluation results to coaching sessions and tracks improvement over time. A complementary[workforce management solution](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/workforce-management/) can help ensure you have the right staffing in place to act on those coaching insights.
7. **Review analytics and reporting depth.** Look for dashboards that surface trends at the team, agent, and interaction level and that connect quality scores to customer outcome metrics like CSAT and resolution rates.


> **Key question to ask any vendor:** How does your QMS connect evaluation data to coaching outcomes, and what evidence do you have that this connection drives measurable performance improvement?

## What are the top QMS use cases?


A quality management system delivers value across a range of contact center scenarios. Here are five use cases most relevant to Quality Managers and CX leaders:

4. **Omnichannel quality consistency.** Contact centers handling customer interactions across voice, chat, email, and messaging use QMS tools to apply consistent evaluation criteria across every channel, closing the gap between digital and voice service quality.

## Quality management system FAQs


### Q1: What is a quality management system?


A quality management system is a formalized framework of processes, tools, and standards that organizations use to monitor, evaluate, and improve the quality of service delivery. In a contact center, a QMS provides the operational structure for recording customer interactions, scoring agent performance against defined criteria, and connecting evaluation results to coaching and improvement programs.


Contact center QMS platforms have evolved significantly in recent years. Modern systems use AI to evaluate interactions at scale, moving beyond manual review of a limited sample toward greater visibility across voice and digital channels. The shift from sample-based review to more comprehensive interaction coverage is one of the most consequential changes in how contact centers manage service quality today.


### Q2: How does Zoom Contact Center support quality management?


[Zoom Contact Center](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/contact-center/) includes[Zoom Quality Management](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/quality-management/) as a native add-on that uses AI to automatically evaluate customer interactions across voice and digital channels. The platform enables supervisors to review interaction recordings, assess conversations against custom scorecards, surface sentiment signals, and assign targeted coaching sessions, all within the same connected environment where customer interactions take place.


[Zoom CX Insights](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/cx-insights/) extends quality management data into a unified analytics layer, giving Quality Managers and CX leaders visibility into performance trends across teams and channels. Because quality management is built into the Zoom Contact Center platform rather than integrated from a separate vendor, data stays connected and workflows remain streamlined, reducing administrative burden on supervisors and enabling faster coaching cycles.


### Q3: What is the difference between quality assurance and quality management?


Quality assurance (QA) is a component within the broader quality management framework. QA focuses specifically on evaluating individual interactions against defined standards, scoring conversations, flagging compliance issues, and identifying where an agent deviated from expected behavior. Quality management encompasses QA plus the upstream and downstream processes: scorecard design, calibration, coaching workflows, trend analysis, and ongoing improvement planning.


In practice, many contact centers use the terms interchangeably, but the distinction matters when evaluating technology. A system that only handles QA doesn't address how those scores translate into agent development. A full quality management system connects evaluation data to coaching outcomes, making performance improvement a measurable process rather than a periodic review activity.


### Q4: What key metrics does a quality management system track?


A quality management system tracks a combination of interaction-level and aggregate performance metrics. At the interaction level, common metrics include scorecard scores, compliance adherence rates, sentiment signals, and resolution outcomes. At the team and agent level, QMS analytics typically surface average evaluation scores, coaching completion rates, first contact resolution, customer satisfaction (CSAT), and average handle time (AHT).


The metrics a QMS captures are most useful when connected to customer outcome data, linking agent evaluation scores to CSAT or NPS trends, for example. Contact centers that track quality metrics in isolation from customer outcomes often find it difficult to demonstrate the business impact of coaching investments. Modern QMS platforms increasingly provide this cross-metric visibility in a single reporting interface.


### Q5: How does AI improve quality management in contact centers?


AI improves quality management in contact centers by expanding the scope of what teams can evaluate. Traditional QM programs rely on supervisors manually reviewing a small portion of recorded interactions. AI-powered QMS platforms apply automated scoring to a much larger share of interactions across voice and digital channels, surfacing patterns, coaching opportunities, and compliance risks that manual review may miss at scale.


AI also enables more consistent scoring. Human reviewers can apply criteria differently across reviewers and over time AI evaluates interactions against consistent standards, reducing scoring variance and improving calibration. The combination of broader coverage and more consistent evaluation can support a more comprehensive view of team performance and a stronger foundation for targeted coaching. Human oversight remains essential throughout: supervisors should retain the ability to review, calibrate, and override AI-generated scores.


### Q6: What should contact center managers look for in QMS software?


Contact center managers should prioritize QMS software that integrates natively with their core platform, supports omnichannel interaction evaluation, and connects evaluation data directly to coaching workflows. Configurable scorecards, AI-powered scoring, and compliance monitoring capabilities are widely considered essential for modern contact center operations. The most critical differentiator is how well the system turns evaluation data into measurable agent performance improvement.


Beyond feature evaluation, managers should assess implementation requirements, calibration capabilities, and the vendor's approach to AI oversight. Confirm that supervisors retain the ability to review, override, and calibrate AI-generated scores. A system that evaluates interactions at scale but provides no mechanism for human review introduces new risks even as it reduces others. Ask vendors for evidence of coaching outcome data tied to QMS use before making a final decision.
